property_summary: For every interfaceId input, the correct contract C returns true from supportsInterface when queried for either IAccessControl or IERC165 (i.e., it returns true for IERC165.interfaceId and for IAccessControl.interfaceId), while the mutant returns false for IERC165.interfaceId, so there exists an interfaceId (the IERC165 id) where their return values differ.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference contract's supportsInterface returns true for IERC165.interfaceId and for IAccessControl.interfaceId; the mutant returns false for IERC165.interfaceId, so querying supportsInterface with type(IERC165).interfaceId yields true on the reference but false on the mutant.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference C reports supportsInterface(interfaceId)==true whenever interfaceId equals type(IAccessControl).interfaceId or type(IERC165).interfaceId; the mutant breaks this by returning false for type(IERC165).interfaceId, so there exists an interfaceId (IERC165) where the reference returns true but the mutant returns false.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true when interfaceId equals type(IAccessControl).interfaceId or type(IERC165).interfaceId; the mutant returns false for type(IERC165).interfaceId, so querying supportsInterface with a fuzzed bytes4 that equals type(IERC165).interfaceId yields differing results.

For every bytes4 id, C.supportsInterface(id) returns true when id == type(IERC165).interfaceId or id == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId; the mutant returns false for type(IERC165).interfaceId, so querying supportsInterface with a fuzzed bytes4 that can equal type(IERC165).interfaceId distinguishes them.

For every 4-byte interfaceId the reference contract's supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true exactly when that interfaceId equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (or when super supportsInterface would return true), whereas the mutant always returns false; therefore the reference will return true for at least one interfaceId (e.g. IERC165) for all deployments while the mutant will return false for that same input—so there exists interfaceIds where values differ.

For any interfaceId equal to IERC165's interfaceId, the correct contract's supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true (since it checks IERC165 and IAccessControl via super), whereas the mutant always returns false, so there exists an input interfaceId (the IERC165 id) where the mutant's return differs.

For every 4-byte interfaceId the reference contract reports support for IERC165 (i.e. supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) returns true), whereas the mutant always returns false, so there exists an interfaceId (the IERC165 interface id) for which the reference returns true but the mutant returns false.

For every 4-byte interfaceId the reference C reports support for the ERC165 interface id (type(IERC165).interfaceId) — i.e. supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) returns true — whereas the mutant always returns false, so there exists an interfaceId (the ERC165 id) where the mutant's return differs.

For every 4-byte interfaceId, calling supportsInterface(interfaceId) on the correct contract never reverts and returns the same value as calling supportsInterface(interfaceId) on its ERC165 super (i.e. honors ERC165 behavior via super.supportsInterface); the mutant breaks this by always returning false for some interfaceIds that the reference reports true for (so there exist interfaceIds where the two return values differ).

For every interfaceId, the reference contract returns true exactly when the interfaceId equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (via ERC165/super) as implemented; the mutant that always returns true will report support for other arbitrary ids too, so there exist interfaceIds where reference.supportsInterface(id) != mutant.supportsInterface(id).

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference C returns true from supportsInterface(bytes4) iff that id equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (i.e. C.supportsInterface only returns true for supported interfaces via ERC165 chaining), while the mutant returns true for all ids—so there exist ids for which reference returns false but mutant returns true.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns false for some ids (i.e. it does not claim to support arbitrary random ids), whereas the mutant always returns true — so there exist fuzzed interfaceIds for which reference returns false but the mutant returns true.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference contract's supportsInterface(interfaceId) never returns true for arbitrary ids that are not IERC165 or IAccessControl (i.e. there exist interfaceIds for which it returns false), while the mutant returns true for all ids — so the property: "there exists some interfaceId such that supportsInterface(interfaceId) == false" holds for the reference but is violated by the mutant for those ids.

For every bytes4 interfaceId the reference contract's supportsInterface call never returns true for at least one id (i.e. not all ids are reported supported); the mutant always returns true for every id, violating that property for some fuzzed ids.

For every interfaceId input, the reference contract returns true for IERC165 and IAccessControl interface ids (i.e. supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) == true and supportsInterface(type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) == true for the correct implementation), while the mutant that delegates solely to super.supportsInterface will return false for IAccessControl (breaking the rule for some inputs).

For every interfaceId, the correct contract C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true for the ERC165 interface id and for the IAccessControl interface id (i.e. it supports IERC165 and IAccessControl), whereas the mutant that only calls super.supportsInterface will return false for IAccessControl for some interfaceId inputs, violating that rule.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true when interfaceId equals type(IAccessControl).interfaceId (i.e. C advertises support for IAccessControl), whereas the mutant that only calls super.supportsInterface will not report support for IAccessControl for that interface id.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the correct C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true whenever interfaceId equals type(IAccessControl).interfaceId OR equals type(IERC165).interfaceId; the mutant that only delegates to super.supportsInterface will return true for IERC165 but may return false for IAccessControl, so the property is that supportsInterface reports support for IAccessControl and the mutant breaks that for the IAccessControl id.

For every bytes4 interfaceId input, the correct C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) never returns false for the IERC165 interface id (it always reports support for IERC165); the mutant that removes the direct IAccessControl check still must continue to report IERC165 support, so the universal rule is that supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) == true for all deployments — a call to supportsInterface with the IERC165 id should succeed and return true on the reference, while some mutants that change interface logic may break this invariant.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the correct contract returns true exactly when interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId or when super.supportsInterface(interfaceId) is true, but the mutant flips the equality check causing some interfaceId (notably any value equal to type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) to return the opposite result; thus the property: calling supportsInterface(x) never returns the negation-for-equal-case — specifically, supportsInterface(type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) must be true on the reference but false on the mutant for that input.

For every bytes4 interfaceId the reference contract returns true for IAccessControl's interfaceId (type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) via supportsInterface, whereas the mutant negates that equality so there exists an interfaceId (specifically type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) for which the mutant returns false while the reference returns true.

For every bytes4 interfaceId the correct contract reports support for IAccessControl's interfaceId (supportsInterface(type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) == true), whereas the mutant that negates the equality will return false for that specific interfaceId; the test fuzzes an interfaceId and asserts that if it equals type(IAccessControl).interfaceId then supportsInterface returns true (a property the mutant will violate for that input).

For every bytes4 id, the reference C reports supportsInterface(type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) == true; the mutant negates the equality and will return false for that specific interface id, so fuzzing an arbitrary bytes4 and asserting supportsInterface(type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) is always true distinguishes them.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, calling supportsInterface(interfaceId) on the correct contract returns true whenever super.supportsInterface(interfaceId) is true OR interfaceId equals type(IAccessControl).interfaceId; the mutant flips the equality check so there exists an interfaceId (specifically type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) for which the reference returns true but the mutant returns false.

For any role and account, hasRole(role, account) returns true exactly when the stored mapping _roles[role].members[account] is true; the mutant inverts this and thus will return the opposite for some (role,account) inputs.
